name: Phenylephrine

summary: Vasopressor for clinically important hypotension resulting primarily from vasodilation in the setting of anaesthesia. Nursing focus: angina and heart failure, ischaemia, extravasation necrosis and bradycardia.

items.text: The label indicates phenylephrine hydrochloride injection for the treatment of clinically important hypotension resulting primarily from vasodilation in the setting of anaesthesia.

The registered anaesthesia product indication does not establish a first-line role in septic shock. SSC 2026 names norepinephrine for usual initial support. Any phenylephrine use in another setting requires product-specific indication and clinician assessment.

Inspect the peripheral IV site for pallor, swelling, pain or leakage. If phenylephrine extravasation is suspected, stop delivery through the affected catheter and urgently escalate under the local extravasation plan, coordinating alternative authorised vasopressor access if continued haemodynamic support is required.
Monitoring frequency and alarm limits follow the unit's protocol for this medicine.
The label calls for monitoring of kidney function.

The registered label warns of severe bradycardia, reduced cardiac output, peripheral and visceral ischaemia and renal toxicity; this formulation contains a sulfite. Escalate signs of reduced organ perfusion promptly and review formulation-specific allergy risk.
New bradycardia or declining tissue perfusion after a pressure rise warrants prompt team review; pressure alone is not evidence of restored flow.

Oxytocic medicines, monoamine oxidase inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants may amplify the pressor response. Autonomic dysfunction may also increase sensitivity. Review these exposures with pharmacy and the treating team; report unexpectedly severe hypertension or new neurological symptoms immediately.
It can precipitate angina in patients with severe arteriosclerosis or a history of angina, exacerbate heart failure and increase pulmonary arterial pressure.
It can cause excessive peripheral and visceral vasoconstriction and ischaemia to vital organs.
Extravasation during intravenous administration may cause necrosis or sloughing of tissue.
It can cause severe bradycardia and decreased cardiac output.
Adverse reactions are primarily attributable to excessive pharmacological activity.

The label lists reflex bradycardia, lowered cardiac output, myocardial ischaemia, hypertension (including hypertensive crisis) and arrhythmias as cardiac and vascular adverse reactions, and headache, blurred vision, neck pain, tremor, dyspnoea, itching, epigastric pain, vomiting and nausea as other reported adverse reactions; nausea, vomiting and headache were the most commonly reported.

For suspected extravasation, promptly stop phenylephrine at the compromised IV site, assess skin and perfusion, notify the clinical/pharmacy team, avoid force-flushing, and follow institutional rules on leaving the catheter available for evaluation and obtaining alternative access. Do not generalize this medication's anaesthesia label to a universal ICU prescription. Activate emergency help for severe bradycardia with instability, suspected organ ischaemia or anaphylaxis. Coordinate safe continuity of essential circulatory support through authorised alternative access when an injured site is involved.
Escalate for chest pain, slowing heart rate, falling urine output, cold or mottled limbs, or any extravasation.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record the product and order checks, monitoring results, adverse events and escalation per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Inspect the infusion site for extravasation.
Monitor heart rate, rhythm and blood pressure.
Report chest pain, bradycardia or extravasation immediately.

Assess heart rate, blood pressure and signs of tissue perfusion together; report new bradycardia, worsening perfusion, abdominal pain or renal deterioration even when pressure improves. Verify relevant sulfite allergy history.
Flag oxytocic medicines, interacting antidepressants and autonomic dysfunction; monitor pressure and perfusion.
